vignette:
Darnell is a 61-year-old African American man who has worked as a city bus driver for nearly two decades. He is married, and his wife describes him as someone who, until recently, was steady and dependable - the kind of man who kept his schedule, kept his promises, and kept his feelings largely to himself. That steadiness has been shaken in ways neither of them fully understands, and it was his wife who finally persuaded him to seek help.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Darnell was taken and held by a group of men during what began as a routine layover on an unfamiliar route he had agreed to cover for a colleague. The details of what followed are not something he has been able to recount in sequence. He was restrained in a confined space, subjected to prolonged physical abuse, and forced to witness the same being done to another man - a stranger, someone he did not know and could not help. He does not know how long he was held. He does not know whether the other man survived. These gaps are not chosen silences; they are absences in his own mind, places where the memory simply stops and then resumes somewhere else, like a film with frames cut out. Some moments are still unbearably vivid - the texture of the floor, a particular sound, the smell of the room - while entire stretches of hours remain blank. He has come to believe that the missing pieces must contain something worse than what he can remember, and this belief alone is enough to fill him with dread.

What Darnell carries most heavily is not the physical aftermath but the moral one. He is certain he is a weak man. He had not fought back. He had not called out to the other man, had not done anything he can name as courage. The conviction that he failed to protect someone who was suffering beside him has settled into something close to self-contempt, and he has told his therapist, quietly, that he does not expect to forgive himself. These appraisals of himself as fundamentally inadequate and culpable have made the world feel more dangerous in a specific way: if he failed then, he believes he will fail again. He is not safe to trust, and the world, therefore, is not safe to inhabit. This reasoning - that his own weakness makes threat perpetually likely - has intensified his vigilance in ways that feel logical to him even as they exhaust him.

At night the vigilance is worst. Darnell sleeps lightly if at all, lying still and listening for sounds at the windows or the door, certain that the perimeter of his home is not as secure as it appears. During the day he manages better, but evenings on his bus route - the last runs, when the light drops and the streets empty - carry a particular weight. The sounds of the bus, the confined space, the loss of open visibility: these are the conditions that most reliably bring the physical reactions he cannot control, the sudden flooding of his body with something that feels indistinguishable from the original terror. When those physical reactions surge through him, the memory fragments surface with them, and the terror he felt during the event returns not as a recollection but as a repetition - something happening now rather than then. And each time the memory returns with that force, it confirms for him again that he is broken, that a stronger man would have processed this by now, that his inability to move past it is itself evidence of the weakness he already knew he had.

The loop has tightened over months. His wife has noticed that he no longer speaks about the future. He has requested only daytime routes and offered no explanation his supervisor would accept. He has begun checking the locks on the front door multiple times before bed, a habit his wife watches without comment because she does not know what to say. What finally brought him to seek help was a morning when he sat in the driveway in his uniform for forty minutes, unable to make himself start the bus. What he is most afraid of, he says, is that there is nothing left to recover - that what the event took from him was not temporary. What he is hoping for, though he offers this more quietly, is that someone might tell him he is not the man he has come to believe he is.
